Government debt issuances rose to $42bn during the first six months of 2026 from $37.4bn in the same period of 2025, while corporate issuances increased to $74.8bn from $64.8bn a year earlier.

The report noted that total debt issuances across the GCC had reached a record $212.2bn during full-year 2025.

By instrument type, bond issuances recorded strong growth during the first half of 2026, while sukuk issuances declined sharply.

Aggregate GCC bond issuances totalled $86.4bn during the first six months of 2026, compared with $61.2bn in the corresponding period of 2025. In contrast, sukuk issuances fell by almost a quarter to $30.5bn, down from $41bn during the first half of last year.

At the country level, debt issuances registered broad-based year-on-year growth across the GCC, with the exception of a marginal decline in Bahrain.

The report said refinancing needs are expected to total $30.7bn during the second half of the year, while government borrowing to finance budget deficits amid lower oil revenues is also likely to support issuance activity.

In addition, a series of reforms aimed at diversifying logistics and transportation infrastructure for crude oil trade is expected to generate further fundraising through bonds, sukuks and private placements.

Kamco Investment expects sukuk issuances to regain momentum during the second half of 2026, supported by strong demand from dedicated investors and issuers' efforts to diversify funding sources.

However, the report warned that the principal downside risk remains a re-escalation of regional conflict, which could delay foreign-currency debt issuances and lead to wider credit spreads.

The report also highlighted that GCC governments face elevated debt maturities over the next five years, particularly for bonds issued in the years following the pandemic. According to Bloomberg data, GCC sovereign debt maturities amount to $236.6bn over the 2026-2030 period, while corporate maturities are slightly higher at $254.8bn.

Both bond and sukuk maturities are expected to remain elevated from 2027 through 2031 before gradually tapering over the remainder of the maturity profile. The report attributed the high volume of maturities over the next five years to the significant number of short-term debt issuances, with maturities of less than five years, by both governments and corporates.

Developers would pay when accepting a grid connection offer and recover the money once the project was energised. Those leaving the queue early would forfeit the fee.

Ofgem fears that many of these developments will never proceed but are occupying scarce capacity, delaying investment-ready schemes and distorting decisions about future network spending.

  > Enbridge surveyed about 200 landowners and assigned agents to discuss routing concerns.

Eileen and James Gunipero opened a letter on April 16 from Enbridge Gas North Carolina. The company planned to survey their 22-acre property for a proposed natural gas pipeline.

Soon after, the Guniperos joined hundreds of Chatham County residents opposing the project. With different maps being circulated in the community, residents still don't know, months later, whether the pipeline would cross their property, or whether wetlands, culturally significant land or farms they've spent decades caring for would be disturbed.

"We're almost always kept in the dark, and it causes anxiety," Eileen Gunipero told The News & Observer.

On July 17, about 40 people gathered at the Chatham Community Library in Pittsboro, where the Haw River Assembly environmental group hosted a meeting on the pipeline's permitting process and strategies to oppose the project. Attendees discussed eminent domain laws and the proposed data center that many believe is driving demand for the pipeline.

"We're going to be working together to stop this pipeline," Emily Sutton, executive director of the Haw River Assembly, told the crowd as she outlined next steps.

Persida Montanez, spokesperson with Enbridge, told The N&O that the company needs the 28-mile pipeline to meet growing residential and business demand in Chatham and Lee counties. The company has surveyed about 200 landowners and says each has been assigned an agent to discuss routing and property concerns.

Montanez said the number of customers it serves in Chatham County increased 2.7% over the past year, one of the fastest-growing counties in its service territory.

During the community meeting, Sutton told attendees that Enbridge cannot apply for environmental permits until a route is finalized. She said the Army Corps of Engineers relies heavily on company-funded archaeological surveys and suggested residents consider hiring their own experts to document culturally significant sites before the route is complete and permits are issued.

She also urged residents to ask the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality to require individual permits for each stream and wetland crossing instead of issuing one general permit. Once Enbridge does apply for permits, DEQ has 15 days to review an application followed by another 15 days to consider public comments.

'Our property is being usurped'

The Guniperos moved from New York to Chatham County with their Icelandic horses in 2007. The property was intended to be a long-term retirement property and family farm compound after James, 72, retired as a podiatric surgeon and Eileen, 71, from administrative work and running an Icelandic horse tack store.

The proposed pipeline, 12 inches in diameter, would stretch from Siler City to Moncure. The Guniperos said Enbridge has downplayed the long-term restrictions that easements could place on their land. For instance, the pipeline would prohibit families from farming or building on their land, and Enbridge would own the right to expand the pipeline at any time without resident input.

The typical permanent easement is expected to be 50 feet wide, according to Montanez. Additionally, an easement would allow Enbridge to operate and maintain the pipeline, but would not transfer ownership of the property, she noted.

"It just feels like our property is being usurped," Eileen Gunipero said. "The area of the farm that is most threatened by the pipeline still has the survey flags evident from recent work to subdivide approximately two acres that were intended for a young couple we consider family."

"It was envisioned that we would have several members of the family living here as we age," she explained. "The newly surveyed section would not be used should the pipeline come through."

Eminent domain

Governments can use eminent domain to acquire private property for projects that are deemed to benefit the public. They must pay the landowners for their property. Private utility companies can also use eminent domain for purposes such as pipelines.

Montanez said Enbridge is "committed to doing all we can to work with property owners to reach a positive outcome."

James Gunipero said he understands the purpose of eminent domain, "but to me it seems that corporations are twisting it and using it more as legalized thievery."

Many residents have also questioned whether the project primarily serves future industrial development rather than existing residents.

"We all use propane or solar or a mixture of both. But very few of us use natural gas," Chatham resident Jenna Dunning told The N&O. "It's not a public need."

Among other concerns, the Guniperos are worried about leaks and pollution during the process of installing the pipeline.

"We don't know what can be left over. [Enbridge doesn't] exactly have the best track record for any of this, and I'm not convinced they would do anything in our favor. Once they leave that pipeline in, we're living on a landmine, essentially," James said.

Enbridge, a Canadian energy infrastructure company, owns gas and energy divisions across North America, including Enbridge Gas North Carolina. The company has a controversial history in Wisconsin. The Bad River Band of Lake Superior Chippewa sued the company over its 41-mile oil pipeline after it crossed into tribal land. A federal judge ruled in 2023 the company has trespassed on the reservation since 2013 and ordered it to reroute.

Separately, in 2024, Enbridge detected a crude oil spill of 70,000 gallons in a small town in Wisconsin, prompting cleanup efforts that cost $1.1 million. And in 2019, Wisconsin regulators accused the company of violating state law by waiting more than 15 months to report a pipeline leak near Fort Atkinson that released 1,200 gallons of petroleum into groundwater.

In Chatham County, Enbridge has operated safely since 1955, according to Montanez.

'Over my dead body'

For 85-year-old Dorasue Christian, the pipeline threatens more than just her property.

Christian, a widow, lives on 22.5 acres with her 66-year-old son, who has a disability. The property, which her family has owned for generations, is filled with chickens, birds, a pond and wildlife that she says provide the quiet environment her son depends on.

She also worries construction could cross beneath her pond and permanently alter the land.

"I've never been arrested in my life. ... I've never even had a parking ticket," she told The N&O. "If Enbridge takes this land, they're going to have to come over my dead body."

Christian, who retired as a dental hygienist in 2001, has said she is running out of savings and had planned to sell parcels of her land to support her son, but she said if Enbridge constructs a pipeline through it, buyers will not want to purchase it, due to the liability.

At the community meeting, residents repeatedly discussed the prospect that the pipeline would cross creeks, rivers and tributaries.

Retired biologist John Alderman, who is currently being sued by Enbridge, has been vocal in saying the pipeline would threaten the Rocky River-Deep River system, which is a habitat for the federally endangered Cape Fear Shiner fish. In a letter to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, he urged them to prepare an environmental impact statement, warning that the pipeline would increase sedimentation and erosion, require blasting, contribute to unwarranted deforestation and affect water runoff, among other issues.

Crystal Cavalier-Keck of 7 Directions of Service, an Indigenous-led environmental justice organization, told The N&O the proposed route also crosses documented Tuscarora village sites. She said many Tuscarora live in New York and have lost a bond to North Carolina. She believes the pipeline could cut any connections Tuscarora have left to their land.

"It's just really all about trying to connect back to our ancestors and our way of being as Indigenous people, because that really reminds us of the sacred responsibilities given to us from the Creator, and so when people start to lose that connection they really start to lose respect for everything -- the environment, the animals, the other people," she said.

Montanez said any concerns with cultural sites and farms will be addressed before the final route is selected.

"We take cultural and archaeological resources really seriously," she said. "The route has not been finalized, and the intent is to avoid environmental and cultural resources to the greatest extent possible."

Enbridge held an open house July 28 that gave residents an opportunity to provide feedback on the route to land agents.

In a public packet provided to The N&O, Enbridge wrote that residents may receive additional survey notifications, requests for property access and potential easement discussions as the next steps. For larger rivers and sensitive areas, the company wrote it would consider horizontal directional drilling, a trenchless construction method that bores beneath the water to reduce surface disturbance.

Enbridge denies data center claims

Near the end of the July 17 meeting residents said the pipeline may have ties to a proposed 740-megawatt EcoTip data center planned for Chatham County.

The data center would include cryptocurrency mining and is managed by Kirk Bradley, owner and CEO of real estate firm Lee Moore Capitol Co.

Montanez disputed this claim, and told The N&O the pipeline will not support a data center, and could not do so because the gas that would flow through its 12-inch diameter pipe would not support the level of energy a data center demands.

Still, residents feel Enbridge hasn't been transparent.

Dunning said the study corridor map stops directly at the EcoTip site where the proposed data center may go.

"That's not a public need, that's an industrial need, but if that is the case, then eminent domain is not justified," she said.

Dunning also pointed to Enbridge's 2025 annual report, which says the company's long-term strategy is to expand natural gas infrastructure and mentions data centers as a driver of future pipeline development.

"We continue to work with customers on opportunities to supply gas for new power generation that supports data centers and overall demand growth, and capitalize on strong gas fundamentals to deliver safe, reliable, and lower-carbon energy to North Americans while simultaneously growing (liquified natural gas) exports," the document said.

Still, in a frequently asked questions section on the company's website, it denies that the proposed pipeline could support a data center and says "no such request has been made to date."

Chatham County Manager Bryan Thompson told The N&O the county will evaluate the pipeline project to determine its role under applicable law and potential impacts.

"The County has received many comments from residents expressing concerns about the proposed Enbridge pipeline project," he said in an email.

In response, the Chatham County Board of Commissioners has scheduled a meeting on Aug. 5 to receive further public comment on the pipeline.

- **2026-07-29** [BofA says Fed hike today would be one for the books](https://www.fresnobee.com/news/business/article316698524.html) — The Fresno Bee (relevance 0.25)
  > Central banks spend decades building a reputation and can spend the whole thing in a single afternoon.

Every institution that manages expectations for a living runs into the same trap. Move too slowly and you look asleep at the wheel. Move without warning and you teach everyone watching that your signals were never worth much.

The Federal Reserve has kept its benchmark rate parked in a range of 3.5% to 3.75% since December, holding at four consecutive meetings while inflation stayed stubbornly above the 2% target, according to the Federal Reserve. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has promised price stability without saying much about how he intends to deliver it.

Crude oil has made that promise harder to keep, running up roughly 20% across July before pulling back sharply this week, according to Kiplinger.

So the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) walks into the afternoon of July 29 with a question that has not been genuinely open in years. Not whether to cut. Whether to raise.

And if the committee does raise, it will be doing something it has not done once since 1994, according to Bank of America (BAC).

Tom Williams / Getty Images

How the Fed tells you what it is about to do

The Fed does not really surprise anybody anymore, and that is by design.

Long before a decision lands, policymakers give speeches, testify to Congress, and publish minutes. Traders take all of it and push money into federal funds futures, contracts that pay out based on where the benchmark rate actually settles.

Add those bets up and you get a percentage. That number is what people mean when they say a move is "priced in."

The reason the Fed watches that number so closely is that surprises are expensive. When a central bank moves in a direction markets have not funded, positions unwind all at once, and the damage lands somewhere nobody intended.

That is the backdrop against which Warsh has spent his first two months as chair. The June meeting produced a unanimous hold, but the minutes showed a committee already arguing about which direction the next move goes.

Cooler June inflation looked, briefly, like it had settled the question, as TheStreet reported. Then oil turned.

Bank of America says a July hike would be unprecedented

Here is the part that reframes the whole debate.

Reviewing federal funds futures data going back to 1994, the bank found that the Fed has never once hiked rates with less than 60% priced in beforehand, according to Bank of America. Markets have priced roughly 10 basis points of tightening into Wednesday, the bank said, which works out to well under half that threshold.

A move this week would be "unprecedented," according to Bank of America, and would establish "Warsh credibility on independence & inflation."

More Federal Reserve:

The bank's base case is still a hold, with two hike dissents expected from Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, though a move higher "can't be ruled out," said BofA rates strategist Mark Cabana.

What struck me when I ran BofA's threshold against this week's pricing is how wide the gap actually is. Traders are giving a hike roughly 38% odds, according to the CME Group FedWatch Tool. Every hike of the past 32 years arrived with at least 60% behind it.

That is not a small miss. In my analysis, it is the difference between a Fed that follows the market and a Fed that decides the market has been reading it wrong.

What a quarter-point move does to your borrowing costs

Strip away the mechanics and a rate decision is a bill.

The federal funds rate sets what banks charge each other overnight. That feeds the prime rate, which sets your credit card APR, your home equity line, and most variable-rate debt you carry. A quarter-point hike shows up on card statements inside one or two billing cycles.

Mortgages work differently. Thirty-year rates track the 10-year Treasury yield, which responds less to the decision itself than to what Warsh says about the path ahead at his 2:30 p.m. press conference.

Savers get the other side of it. Higher benchmark rates push up yields on high-yield savings accounts and certificates of deposit, usually with a lag of a few weeks.

The dollars are smaller than the drama suggests. A quarter point on an $8,000 credit card balance runs about $20 a year. On a $50,000 home equity line, closer to $125.

That math changes if July 29 is the first of several. BofA said a hike now would pull forward expected 2026 tightening from about 45 basis points to roughly 60, according to Bank of America.

Where things stand going in:

* Current target range: 3.5% to 3.75%, held by a 12 to 0 vote in June, according to the Federal Reserve.

* Minimum priced-in level before any Fed hike since 1994: 60%, according to Bank of America.

* Tightening priced into Wednesday's meeting: roughly 10 basis points, according to Bank of America.

* Market-implied odds of a quarter-point hike: near 38%, according to the CME Group FedWatch Tool.

* Crude oil's July move: up roughly 20% for the month, according to Kiplinger.

The oil line is doing more work than it looks. Energy costs bleed into transportation, food, and utilities on a lag, which is why a barrel of crude ends up in a grocery bill two months later.

Why September may matter more than today

Skip the headline number and read the vote count instead.

A unanimous hold tells you the committee is comfortable waiting. A hold with two or three dissents tells you the hawks are organizing, and that September, the next scheduled meeting, becomes the real fight.

There is no August meeting, which means whatever the Fed does Wednesday stands for roughly seven weeks regardless of what oil or inflation does in the meantime.

BofA is positioned for the consequences either way. The bank said it remains paid on the two-year Treasury, holds 2s10s flatteners, and is bullish on the dollar, according to Bank of America.

For everyone else, the practical move is smaller and duller. If you carry a variable-rate balance, a hike makes paying it down more valuable this month than last. If you have cash sitting in a checking account earning nothing, a hawkish Warsh press conference is your cue to go shopping for yield.

The record BofA dug up does not tell you what the Fed will do. It tells you what it would cost the Fed to do it, and that is usually the better thing to watch.

- **2026-07-29** [Balance between food and fuel security](https://www.hindustantimes.com/editorials/balance-between-food-and-fuel-security-101785339776815.html) — Hindustan Times (relevance 0.25)
  > The debate around India's biofuel blending push has mostly focused on the alleged harmful effects of the fuel being sold on cars. This is perhaps the easiest of the controversies to solve, provided the government lays down clear cut guidelines for fuel retailers and car producers. India is not the only country where biofuel is blended with fossil fuels.

The larger and more difficult questions around the biofuel industry are rooted in the political economy of maintaining a balance between food and fuel needs of the country. An HT report from the ongoing Parliament proceedings offers a glimpse into this larger tension.

The government, while answering a question in the Rajya Sabha said that the Food Corporation of India (FCI) sold rice at a discount -- around 40% less than the average acquisition cost of the agency -- to distillers for producing ethanol. While the government did not provide details on the end use of the ethanol produced by using this discounted sale, it is likely that a substantial part of the produce could have been used for fuel blending requirements.

This raises a larger question about the biofuel blending industrial complex in the economy. Because the raw material required for producing the blend is the same as the country's food and feed requirements, a growing diversion to fuel use without a corresponding increase in production will entail a pressure on supplying to the food and feed demand. Left to the open market, this can either lead to an increase in food/feed prices or make the cost of fuel blending prohibitively high. Some of India's government owned fuel retailing officials have come on record that ethanol blending is not necessarily a cost saving method, although it might save the country precious foreign exchange in importing crude oil. Given this backdrop, how judicious is FCI's discounted sales to ethanol producers?

FCI's procurement budget comes out India's food security bill. This is aggressively watched by countries and multilateral agencies such as the US and the WTO. Using this money to subsidise fuel blending creates unwarranted pressure on India's agricultural support and food security programmes. Ideally, the money should be earmarked as fuel subsidy.

The more important question is not classifying subsidies. It is whether India's biofuel blending ambitions have taken note of the larger tensions between securing food-feed-fuel needs of the economy.

Trade has subtracted from GDP for two straight quarters.

The Census Bureau report showed wholesale inventories increased 0.3% in June, matching May's gain. Stocks at retailers were unchanged after rising 0.5% in May, though inventories at motor vehicle and parts dealers increased 0.4%.

- **2026-07-28** [The illusion of bigger allocations: Why more Naira does not always mean more wealth - By Kris Ayanruoh - TheNewsGuru](https://thenewsguru.ng/opinion/the-illusion-of-bigger-allocations-why-more-naira-does-not-always-mean-more-wealth-by-kris-ayanruoh/) — TheNewsGuru (relevance 0.25)
  > ...understanding the difference between nominal revenue, purchasing power, and real economic progress in Nigeria's public finances

By Dr. Kris Odafe Ayanruoh

In recent months, Nigerians have repeatedly been reminded that the federal, state, and local governments are receiving more money from the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) than at any other time in the country's history.

Official communiqués have announced record monthly distributions running into trillions of naira. Senior government officials have cited these figures as evidence that recent fiscal reforms are yielding results, while President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has urged governors to ensure that these larger allocations translate into visible improvements in the lives of citizens.

The figures are not imaginary. They are real. Yet they tell only part of the story.

The danger in economic discourse is not always falsehood; sometimes it is incompleteness. A statistic can be entirely accurate and still create a misleading impression if it is stripped of the context necessary for proper interpretation. That is precisely the risk with the growing celebration of record FAAC allocations.

This article does not dispute that governments are receiving more naira than before. They undoubtedly are. The more important question is whether those larger allocations actually represent greater wealth, stronger purchasing power, or improved capacity to deliver public services.

That distinction lies at the heart of sound economics.

There is an old saying that numbers never lie. That is true. But numbers can easily mislead when they answer one question while the audience assumes they are answering another.

When government officials announce that allocations have reached historic levels, many Nigerians naturally conclude that governments have become significantly richer. It is an understandable assumption. After all, if a state received ₦25 billion a month a few years ago and now receives ₦55 billion, common sense suggests that the state should possess far greater financial capacity.

Economics, however, teaches a more nuanced lesson. The first principle every student of economics learns is the distinction between nominal value and real value.

Nominal value measures money in absolute terms. Real value measures what that money can actually buy. This difference may appear academic until it is illustrated with everyday experience.

Imagine that in 2022 you earned ₦500,000 every month. Three years later your salary rises to ₦700,000. Friends congratulate you on your pay increase. On paper you appear substantially wealthier.

But suppose that during those same three years your rent doubled, food prices increased by eighty percent, transportation costs tripled, electricity tariffs rose sharply, school fees escalated, and healthcare became considerably more expensive.

Are you richer?

Your bank statement says yes. Your household budget says otherwise. This is precisely the dilemma facing public finance in Nigeria today.

Governments are receiving larger quantities of naira, but the value of each naira has changed dramatically. Understanding why requires examining the sources of government revenue.

Nigeria earns a significant proportion of its public income from crude oil exports. Oil is sold internationally in United States dollars, not in naira. Consequently, every dollar earned from crude exports must eventually be converted into naira before it is distributed through FAAC.

Here is where exchange rates become critically important. Suppose Nigeria earns US$1 billion from crude oil exports. If one dollar exchanges for ₦430, that revenue becomes approximately ₦430 billion.

If exactly the same US$1 billion is converted at ₦1,500 to one dollar, it suddenly becomes approximately ₦1.5 trillion.

Notice what has happened. Nigeria did not discover more oil. It did not increase production. It did not attract additional foreign investment. It simply converted the same amount of dollars into a weaker domestic currency.

On paper, government revenue has increased dramatically. In reality, the country has not earned a single additional dollar.

This phenomenon is one of the least understood aspects of public finance in Nigeria. Larger naira allocations are often interpreted as evidence of greater national prosperity when, in many cases, they partly reflect the mathematical consequence of currency depreciation.

The removal of fuel subsidies and the liberalisation of the foreign exchange market undoubtedly altered the fiscal landscape. More revenue now flows into the Federation Account, and exchange-rate adjustments have significantly increased the naira value of foreign-currency earnings. These developments explain much of the increase in monthly FAAC distributions.

But higher nominal revenue should never automatically be equated with higher real wealth.

Consider Delta State. In 2022, the state's average monthly FAAC allocation was approximately ₦38.8 billion. At the prevailing official exchange rate, that represented roughly US$90 million.

By 2025, the state's average monthly allocation had increased to approximately ₦54 billion. On paper, that appears to represent impressive growth.

Yet when converted into dollars using the prevailing exchange rate, the allocation was worth only about US$35 million.

The state was receiving substantially more naira while simultaneously possessing far less international purchasing power.

The implication is profound. Governments do not spend statistics. They purchase goods and services.

Modern governance depends heavily on products that are imported directly or priced according to international markets. MRI scanners, CT scanners, pharmaceuticals, laboratory equipment, road construction machinery, electricity infrastructure, aviation components, telecommunications hardware, educational technology, and industrial equipment all depend, directly or indirectly, on foreign exchange.

If a hospital required a diagnostic machine costing US$500,000 in 2022, that machine still costs approximately US$500,000 today.

The difference is that governments now require far more naira to purchase it.

The same reality affects road construction.

Bitumen, heavy equipment, specialised engineering components, steel products, and many construction inputs either originate abroad or are influenced by international pricing.

Consequently, a state receiving ₦55 billion today may not be able to build significantly more roads than it could with ₦40 billion several years ago.

The illusion lies in confusing quantity of currency with economic capacity. Inflation intensifies this challenge. Even goods produced entirely within Nigeria have experienced dramatic price increases.

Contractors pay more for cement. Transporters pay more for diesel. Manufacturers pay more for electricity. Businesses pay more for financing. Workers demand higher wages to cope with rising living costs.

Governments therefore require considerably larger budgets merely to maintain the same level of public services previously delivered.

This is why economists distinguish between nominal growth and real growth. Nominal growth measures the increase in money values. Real growth measures the increase in actual economic capacity after adjusting for inflation.

The distinction is not merely technical. It determines whether a nation is genuinely progressing or simply counting larger quantities of depreciated currency. This brings us to an important point that deserves recognition.

Government officials are not necessarily wrong when they celebrate larger FAAC allocations. The allocations have indeed increased.

Official records confirm that monthly distributions to the three tiers of government are substantially higher than they were several years ago.

President Tinubu has consistently argued that these increased revenues should translate into better governance and improved living standards. Likewise, the Minister of Finance has repeatedly announced record FAAC distributions, highlighting the unprecedented amounts now being shared among federal, state, and local governments.

These statements are factually correct. Where the discussion requires greater balance is in what those figures actually represent.

Receiving more naira does not necessarily mean possessing greater purchasing power.

Receiving larger allocations does not automatically indicate stronger fiscal health.

Receiving record revenues does not guarantee improved development outcomes.

All three propositions can be true simultaneously. This is where public debate should mature.

Rather than asking whether allocations have increased, Nigerians should ask different questions.

How many additional kilometres of roads have been constructed?

How many new classrooms have been built?

How many hospitals have been equipped?

How many primary healthcare centres are functioning effectively?

How much private investment has been attracted?

How many jobs have been created?

How many communities now enjoy reliable water supply?

How much has agricultural productivity increased?

How much has poverty declined?

These are the indicators that determine whether public revenue has been transformed into public value. Numbers entering government accounts are inputs. Development outcomes are outputs.

History offers valuable lessons. Countries experiencing high inflation often report spectacular increases in government revenue measured in local currency.

Argentina has experienced periods during which tax revenues increased dramatically in pesos while citizens became poorer because inflation outpaced income growth.

Zimbabwe once recorded astonishing increases in government revenues expressed in Zimbabwean dollars, even as the currency collapsed and purchasing power evaporated.

No serious economist interpreted those larger nominal figures as evidence of genuine prosperity. Nigeria is not Zimbabwe, nor is it Argentina. But the economic principle remains identical.

A depreciating currency can create the appearance of fiscal expansion without producing a corresponding increase in real economic capacity.

This is why international organisations frequently analyse economies using constant prices, inflation-adjusted values, and dollar-denominated comparisons.

These measures are not intended to diminish government achievements. They are intended to measure reality more accurately.

Another dimension deserves attention. If governments are indeed receiving historically large allocations, citizens are entitled to expect historically better governance.

Larger allocations should produce better roads.

Better schools.

Better hospitals.

Better security.

Better water systems.

Better transportation.

Better sanitation.

Better public administration.

The conversation therefore should not end with the announcement of higher allocations. It should begin there.

Fiscal transparency should evolve beyond announcing how much money governments receive. It should include comprehensive reporting on how effectively those resources improve human welfare.

Citizens deserve to know not only how much entered public accounts but also what those funds accomplished.

Did maternal mortality decline?

Did learning outcomes improve?

Did travel times reduce because of better infrastructure?

Did access to healthcare expand?

Did unemployment fall?

Did productivity increase?

Ultimately, these are the questions that define successful governance.

Perhaps the most constructive way to understand the present debate is to recognise that both supporters and critics of government have legitimate points.

The government is correct that FAAC allocations have reached unprecedented nominal levels.

Critics are equally correct that inflation and exchange-rate depreciation have significantly eroded the purchasing power of those allocations.

These positions are not contradictory. They describe different dimensions of the same economic reality.

Public discourse becomes healthier when both perspectives are acknowledged. Economic progress cannot be measured solely by counting larger bundles of currency.

True prosperity is reflected in stronger purchasing power, improved productivity, rising incomes, expanding opportunities, and better quality of life.

The purpose of public finance is not to produce impressive statistics. It is to improve human welfare. That is why the success of fiscal reforms should ultimately be judged not by the size of monthly FAAC announcements but by the transformation they produce in the lives of ordinary Nigerians.

History teaches a simple lesson.

Prosperous nations are not built by printing larger numbers on weaker currency. They are built by increasing the real value of production, strengthening institutions, improving productivity, attracting investment, and converting public resources into measurable improvements in human development.

As Nigeria continues its economic reforms, it is essential that the nation celebrates progress where it exists while also measuring that progress honestly.

There is nothing wrong with celebrating larger allocations. There is something incomplete about celebrating them without asking what they are truly worth.

For in economics, as in life, wealth is never measured merely by how much money one possesses. It is measured by what that money can actually accomplish.

Dr. Kris Odafe Ayanruoh

Leadership scholar, engineer, and public policy commentator focused on governance, institutional reform, and economic development.

  > Thursday delivers euro-area second-quarter growth at 09:00 GMT and a Bank of England decision at 11:00 GMT, with a fresh forecast round and a press briefing attached.

The Euro is on track for its eighth gain in nine sessions against the Pound, and the explanation that would normally cover a run of that length is not available. Bank Rate sits 150 basis points above the European Central Bank deposit rate, precisely where it has sat since the middle of June, and that spread is what dragged this cross to a one-year low in the first place. The gap has not moved. The cross has.

The spread that never narrowed

Currencies do not trade the rate differential printed on the screen. They trade the one the forward curve expects to exist in six months, which is how a cross can sit still for weeks under an enormous posted gap and then travel a full percent while that gap is unchanged. Since the middle of July the expected differential has narrowed steadily, and almost all of that narrowing has come from the British side.

The mid-July low just over 0.8450 marked the point of maximum agreement that the Bank of England would stay restrictive for longer than the European Central Bank. That view has been taken apart in stages since, mostly by British data and partly by a European central bank that has quietly told the market it has more to do.

One committee is loading while the other unloads

The European Central Bank held at 2.25% on 23 July, unanimously, then used the press briefing to make a September move sound close to inevitable. The President disclosed that some Governing Council members had asked whether rates should rise immediately, and warned that the longer energy costs stay elevated, the more likely they are to leak into broader prices through second-round effects. Roughly 70% odds of a quarter-point September move are now priced, with fresh staff projections landing at that meeting.

The Bank of England arrives on Thursday with the opposite problem. June Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation cooled to 2.6% with services down to 3.6%, pay growth is decelerating, and forecasters expect the new Monetary Policy Report to show inflation peaking near 3% later this year. That projected peak is the whole argument, because a peak nearer 4% has previously been treated as the point at which second-round effects become statistically likely. A forecast topping out a full percentage point below that line disarms the Committee's own hawks.

Both tightening cases rest on the same barrel of Crude Oil, which is the part nobody is pricing consistently. The Gulf stand-down has pulled energy well off its July highs and weakened the inflation impulse on both sides of the Channel, and yet only one front end has repriced for it.

What the Pound was actually paid for in July

July was the best month the Pound has had in years, and it stood on three legs. Political risk unwound as an uncontested succession replaced the contest markets had feared, speculative shorts covered into the move, and traders held a firm expectation of another Bank of England hike before year-end.

Two of those legs have already been collected. The political premium was released the day Andy Burnham walked into Downing Street, and the hike expectation has been draining away since the June inflation print. What is left is carry, a thin defence for a currency heading into an October Budget with the highest long-end government yields in the Group of Seven behind it and borrowing above the official forecast.

Positioning tells the same story from the other end. One widely watched measure had the Pound more technically stretched against the Euro than at any point since before the Brexit referendum, and a July survey of investment banks found a clear majority expecting this cross back into the 0.8700 to 0.8900 area through 2027. Crowded trades do not need bad news to unwind, only the absence of fresh good news.

Thursday does the deciding

Thursday opens at 09:00 GMT with preliminary euro-area second-quarter growth, consensus 0.2% QoQ against a 0.2% contraction previously and 0.5% YoY from 0.3%. Unemployment is seen holding at 6.2% and the Economic Sentiment Indicator improving to 96 from 95. Friday adds the euro-area flash inflation estimate, headline seen at 2.9% YoY from 2.8% with core steady at 2.4%.

The Bank of England follows at 11:00 GMT, consensus a hold at 3.75% on a 7-2 vote, none for a cut and two again preferring 4.00%, with the Monetary Policy Report and minutes attached and a press briefing half an hour later. The hold carries no risk because it is fully priced, which leaves the vote split as the only live variable, and the asymmetry there runs one way. A third hawkish dissent would be a real shock against a forecast round showing a lower peak, while an 8-1 split or a unanimous hold confirms what that forecast already implies.

Technical levels

Resistance: The 50-day Exponential Moving Average just under 0.8600 is the first obstacle, and price has traded beneath it since late June. Above it sits the 0.8600 handle, then the declining 200-day Exponential Moving Average just under 0.8650, the level separating a retracement from a trend change.

Support: The 0.8550 shelf is immediate, defended at the session low just underneath. Beneath that, 0.8500 is the first real test of the recovery, with the mid-July base just over 0.8450 the line that ends it.

Bias: Bullish while above 0.8550, with the daily Stochastic Relative Strength Index turning up out of its July trough and Thursday's event risk skewed toward a softer British outcome. Objectives are the 50-day average just under 0.8600 and then the 0.8600 handle, with 0.8650 the decision point. Invalidation on a daily close back beneath 0.8500.

Bharat Electronics, NTPC, ICICI Bank, Power Grid, and Reliance Industries were also among the laggards. Tata Consultancy Services, Eternal, Tech Mahindra, Infosys, and Titan were among the major gainers.

The BSE SmallCap Select index dipped 0.21 per cent, while MidCap Select index went up 0.35 per cent. Among sectors, capital goods dropped 2.40 per cent, power (2.36 per cent), utilities (1.75 per cent), FMCG (1.27 per cent), industrials (1.22 per cent), energy (0.68 per cent) and commodities (0.68 per cent).

Focused IT jumped 3.44 per cent, IT (3.05 per cent), realty (2.19 per cent), consumer durables (1.32 per cent), auto (0.71 per cent) and consumer discretionary (0.62 per cent). A total of 2,629 stocks declined, while 1,626 advanced and 169 remained unchanged on the BSE.

"The respite in crude oil prices provided relief to markets by easing concerns over inflation and input cost pressures. However, investor sentiment remained cautious ahead of key central bank policy meetings this week, including those of the Fed, BoE (Bank of England), and BoJ (Bank of Japan)," Vinod Nair, Head of Research, Geojit Investments Ltd, said.

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) offloaded equities worth Rs 1,688.23 crore on Monday, according to exchange data. "Indian equity markets ended largely flat as a broad selloff across Asian markets weighed on investor sentiment," Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, an online trading and wealth tech firm, said.

  > Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], July 28 (ANI): The Indian benchmark indices closed a shade lower on Tuesday following a range-bound session amid easing crude oil prices and strong buying across technology stocks.

Sensex settled at 76,765.92, down 69.86 points or 0.09 per cent, while Nifty ended at 23,985.35, down 10.60 points or 0.04 per cent.

The market witnessed mixed sectoral performance with IT leading the gains on strong buying in technology stocks. Majority of broad market indices ended the day's session lower; Nifty IT surged 3.38 per cent followed by Nifty Realty and Midsmall IT & Telecom, surging over 2 per cent. Meanwhile, Nifty FMCG and Bank emerged as top drags, slipping over a per cent.

On BSE, TCS, Eternal, Tech Mahindra, Infosys, Titan, HCL Tech, Asian Paint, M&M, IndiGo, Kotak Bank, Maruti among others were the top gainers. Hindustan Unilever, NTPC, HDFC Bank, Tata Steel, Trent, Axis Bank, Bharti Airtel among others were the top drags.

In the commodity market, Brent crude prices slipped to USD 85 per barrel amid expectations around easing geopolitical tensions between the US and Iran. Brent crude was trading at around USD 85.93 per barrel -- marking the lowest price in a week -- while WTI crude was at around USD 80.77 per barrel at the time of reporting. Gold was trading at around USD 4,023.51 at the same time.

Market analyst Vipin Dixena said, 'Indian benchmark indices witnessed a range-bound and volatile session on Tuesday as investors remained cautious amid mixed global cues. While easing geopolitical tensions and softer crude oil prices offered some support, persistent weakness in global technology stocks and uncertainty ahead of the US Federal Reserve's policy decision kept market participants from taking aggressive positions. The market is likely to remain range-bound in the near term.'

Market participants are exercising caution at the moment, with a pause in hostilities between the US and Iran bringing respite to the energy markets and providing a cushion to the indices. Upcoming central bank policies, especially the US Federal Reserve, will provide broad directions going forward.

Vinod Nair, Head of Research, Geojit Investments Limited said, 'The respite in crude oil prices provided relief to markets by easing concerns over inflation and input cost pressures. However, investor sentiment remained cautious ahead of key central bank policy meetings this week, including those of the Fed, BoE, and BoJ. Persistent volatility in energy markets and heightened geopolitical risks could keep global bond yields elevated this year. Nevertheless, expectations that major central banks will hold interest rates steady in their July policy meetings have offered some support to market sentiment. India's relative advantage under the revised US tariff framework further supported investor confidence.'

Nair expressed optimism on the domestic front with improvement in monsoon conditions as well as moderately better Q1 earnings so far. The surge in IT stocks comes in the backdrop of attractive valuations.

- **2026-07-28** [Senate Moves Graham's Russia Sanctions Bill Forward Amid Tariff Fight](https://www.newsmax.com/newsfront/senate-sanctions-russia/2026/07/28/id/1264279/) — NewsMax (relevance 0.25)
  > A bipartisan group of senators on Tuesday unveiled a compromise sanctions bill backed by President Donald Trump that would expand U.S. penalties on Russia and Iran while granting the president new authority to impose steep tariffs on countries that continue buying Russian energy, Bloomberg reported.

The agreement sets up a renewed fight over presidential trade powers even as lawmakers seek to honor one of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham's final legislative priorities.

The legislation, long championed by Graham, would authorize Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, as well as countries found to be helping Moscow evade energy sanctions.

It would also extend the Iran Sanctions Act through 2031, preventing it from expiring this year, and authorize tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods imported into the United States.

Senate leaders scheduled a procedural vote for Tuesday evening after Trump publicly signaled support for the measure.

The Senate's action comes the same day as Graham's funeral, highlighting the bipartisan push to advance a bill viewed as a cornerstone of the South Carolina Republican's efforts to increase economic pressure on Moscow following Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Although the legislation appears likely to clear the Senate this week, the House has already left Washington for its August recess, delaying final passage until at least September.

Supporters argue the bill would give Trump additional leverage to pressure Russia by targeting one of the Kremlin's most important sources of wartime revenue.

The legislation comes as Trump is scheduled to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the White House on Tuesday. Zelenskyy is also expected to meet lawmakers on Capitol Hill later in the day.

But the bill has exposed a growing partisan divide over its tariff provisions, with some Democrats warning they could inadvertently expand Trump's already aggressive use of executive trade authority.

The dispute centers on language allowing, but not requiring, the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that knowingly purchase Russian crude oil, petroleum products, natural gas, or uranium.

Republicans have argued the flexibility is necessary to secure Trump's backing and ensure the sanctions can be used strategically in negotiations.

Democrats, however, say they are reluctant to give Trump additional discretion over tariffs at a time when they believe he has already exceeded Congress's constitutional role in regulating trade.

Rep. Richard Neal of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, and Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a joint statement last week that they could not support legislation that "hands President Trump a blank check to continue his chaotic tariff agenda."

Their concerns intensified after the Trump administration imposed new tariffs on dozens of U.S. trading partners last week, reinforcing Democrat arguments that Congress should not further broaden the president's unilateral trade authority.

Republicans counter that the sanctions legislation is narrowly tailored and applies only to countries helping finance Russia's war effort.

Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, who has worked to bridge the divide, said lawmakers are exploring language to ensure the tariff authority cannot be interpreted more broadly.

"This legislation is very clear" that the authority applies only to Russian energy sanctions, McCaul said, adding that he would be open to language explicitly reinforcing that limitation if it would ease Democrat concerns.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the bill's lead Democrat co-sponsor, struck an optimistic tone despite the disagreement, saying that "nothing has been this close" to becoming law since he and Graham began working on the sanctions package more than a year ago.

In an effort to win additional support, negotiators also made a last-minute revision limiting the president's new tariff authority to five years.

If ultimately enacted, the legislation would provide the Trump administration with one of its strongest economic tools yet to pressure Moscow while preserving Graham's final major foreign policy initiative.

James Morley III ✉

James Morley III is a writer with more than two decades of experience in entertainment, travel, technology, and science and nature.

  > A member of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) Communication Team, Mr. Wordi David, has called on government to give serious consideration to proposals by the Chamber of Petroleum Consumers (COPEC) and the Chamber of Oil Marketing Companies (COMAC) to review the GH¢1 fuel levy, amid expectations of another increase in fuel prices.

Speaking on the Bubune Breakfast Show hosted by Nana Yaw Asiamah, Mr. David said the issue should be treated as a national concern rather than a partisan debate, as rising fuel prices continue to put pressure on households and businesses.

According to him, both COPEC and COMAC have projected that fuel prices in Ghana are likely to increase due to rising crude oil prices on the international market. In response, COMAC has proposed that government temporarily suspend the GH¢1 fuel levy to cushion consumers against the expected increase.

Mr. David noted that when the levy was introduced, fuel prices were considerably lower. However, with pump prices now climbing because of developments on the global oil market, he believes there is a strong case for government to review the policy.

"People are already struggling with the rising cost of living. If suspending or reducing the GH¢1 levy can provide some relief to consumers, then government should seriously consider it," he said.

He expressed confidence that President John Dramani Mahama would carefully consider the concerns raised by stakeholders through Cabinet deliberations and take a decision that serves the national interest.

Mr. David explained that the GH¢1 fuel levy was introduced to help address longstanding financial challenges in Ghana's energy sector. According to him, the previous administration left behind significant debts, while operational inefficiencies within the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG) further weakened the sector's financial position.

He alleged that multiple accounts created within ECG affected the proper management of energy‑sector revenues, contributing to challenges such as damaged transformers, inadequate maintenance of infrastructure, and persistent operational difficulties.

He said government introduced the levy as a dedicated source of funding to stabilise the energy sector, improve electricity supply, and help prevent recurring power outages.

However, he acknowledged that current market conditions have changed considerably since the levy was introduced.

Mr. David said the proposals by COMAC deserve careful evaluation, stressing that government should explore practical measures that will ease the burden on Ghanaians without undermining efforts to restore financial stability in the energy sector.

While maintaining that the levy was introduced for a legitimate purpose, he argued that the anticipated increase in fuel prices makes a temporary suspension or reduction worthy of consideration.

He concluded by urging the public to remain patient as government consults stakeholders and evaluates the proposals, expressing optimism that any decision reached would strike a balance between protecting consumers and sustaining Ghana's energy sector.

  > THE PESO strengthened further against the dollar on Tuesday as global oil prices continued to go down amid hopes for a end to the Middle East conflict, and after the Philippine central bank chief said more aggressive monetary action remains unlikely despite ongoing global market volatility.

The currency rose by 6.1 centavos to close at P61.614 versus the greenback from its P61.675 finish on Monday, based on data from the Bankers Association of the Philippines' website.

The local unit opened Tuesday's session slightly weaker at P61.70 per dollar. Its best showing was at P61.60, while its intraday low was at P61.76 against the greenback.

Dollars traded went up to $1.16 billion from $990.68 million previously.

"The peso appreciated on increasing prospects of a diplomatic resolution of tensions between the US and Iran after favorable pronouncements from both governments," a trader said in an e-mail.

The peso was also supported by the latest rate hike and currency intervention signals from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) chief, Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. Chief Economist Michael L. Ricafort said in a Viber message.

BSP Governor Eli M. Remolona, Jr. said they could consider a larger 50-basis-point (bp) move amid emerging threats to inflation, but the chance of this happening is small.

He added that the peso's recent slump to a new record low could stoke inflation as it pushes import costs higher. Soaring oil prices amid the fresh flareup in Middle East tensions last week had dragged the peso to a fresh low of P61.847 against the greenback on Friday.

However, he noted that the decline was also due to the broad decline of most currencies against the dollar due to the flight to safety due to developments in the Gulf region.

Mr. Remolona said the BSP intervened minimally during the peso's latest slide to smoothen volatility, but added that trying to defend the currency against a strong dollar is futile as this would only lead to lower reserves.

For Wednesday, the trader sees the peso moving between P61.45 and P61.70 per dollar, likely supported by lower global crude oil prices, while Mr. Ricafort expects it to range from P61.55 to P61.75. -- A.M.C. Sy

Inaction or incremental responses deepen diplomatic isolation and economic costs.   > Mexico exports reached an unprecedented monthly value of US$72,551.0 million in June 2026, according to data released by the national statistics agency INEGI on 27 July. Manufacturing Powers the Surge

Manufacturing exports drove the historic jump, climbing 35.3% year over year to reach US$67,219.0 million in June. The category overwhelmingly dominates Mexico's trade profile, accounting for roughly 93% of all goods shipped abroad during the month.

Non-oil exports, a broader measure that strips out petroleum products, totaled US$70,459.9 million, a 34.1% increase from June 2025. A Widening Trade Surplus

The export boom outpaced a sharp but smaller rise in imports, which grew 28.0% year over year to US$68,461.1 million in June. The gap produced a monthly trade surplus of US$4,089.9 million.

For the first half of 2026, the cumulative surplus reached US$9,857.3 million. Total exports from January through June hit US$389,723.3 million, a 24.6% increase over the same period in 2025. The sustained surplus signals that Mexico is capturing more value from global supply chains than it is spending on foreign inputs.

The Tariff Paradox: US Demand Defies Trade Barriers

Exports to the United States rose 35.8% year over year in June 2026, a striking acceleration that occurred despite new US tariffs on Mexican goods. For foreign investors, this tariff paradox is a critical signal: American industrial demand for Mexican-made components and finished products remains so deeply embedded in cross-border supply chains that it has, so far, absorbed the added cost of trade barriers.

The dynamic reflects the reality that many goods shipped from Mexico are intermediate inputs - auto parts, electronics modules, machinery components - that US factories need to keep production lines running. Tariffs may raise the price, but they have not yet broken the dependency. This resilience is a key reason why the broader Mexico exports figure set a record even as trade policy headwinds intensified.

The Nearshoring Dividend

The record figures reflect a multi-year wave of nearshoring, where foreign companies relocate production from Asia to Mexico to be closer to U.S. consumers. Geopolitical tensions and pandemic-era supply-chain snarls have accelerated the trend, with Mexico's USMCA membership - the trade pact replacing NAFTA - providing a tariff-free gateway to the North American market for qualifying goods.

Industrial parks in northern states such as Nuevo León and Chihuahua have seen vacancy rates plummet. Global automakers, electronics firms, and aerospace suppliers have announced new plants or expansions. The 35.3% leap in manufacturing exports offers the clearest quantitative evidence yet that these projects are translating into physical goods crossing the border. For foreign investors, the data confirms that nearshoring is not a theoretical narrative but a measurable economic force generating hard-currency revenues.

Petroleum and Automotive Components

Petroleum exports totaled US$2,091.1 million in June, a 43.4% year-over-year increase that nonetheless represents a relatively modest share of the overall total. Crude oil accounted for US$1,600.0 million of that sum, while other oil products made up the remaining US$491.1 million. The figures confirm that Mexico's export boom is overwhelmingly a non-petroleum story, reducing the country's historic vulnerability to volatile crude prices.

The INEGI release did not provide a precise June 2026 figure for automotive exports in the supplied research, but the sector remains a cornerstone of Mexico's manufacturing engine. Industry reports consistently identify vehicle and auto-parts shipments as a primary driver of export growth, supported by strong U.S. demand for SUVs and electric-vehicle components.

What the Data Signals for Foreign Investors

For foreign investors, the record numbers validate the thesis that Mexico is a primary beneficiary of supply-chain reconfiguration. A US$9.86 billion half-year surplus suggests the economy is generating foreign exchange organically, which supports currency stability. The Mexican peso, trading near 18.5 to the U.S. dollar, has remained relatively firm.

The breadth of the manufacturing gains indicates that opportunities extend beyond the automotive sector. Electronics, medical devices, and machinery are all contributing to the export surge. Investors examining industrial real estate, logistics, and supplier ecosystems should view the June data as confirmation that demand for Mexican-made goods is accelerating, not plateauing. The tariff paradox - rising exports despite new trade barriers - further suggests that the structural advantages of producing in Mexico are deep enough to withstand policy shocks, a crucial consideration for capital allocation decisions.

Risks and Context

The record figures come with caveats. A 34.4% annual jump partly reflects a comparison against a weaker base month in 2025. Sustaining such growth rates is difficult, and a potential U.S. economic slowdown could dampen demand for Mexican exports.

Additionally, Mexico's reliance on the U.S. market, which absorbs roughly 80% of its exports, remains a concentration risk. Trade policy shifts or new tariffs would disproportionately affect the export sector. Still, the June data provides a strong buffer of momentum as Mexico solidifies its role as a manufacturing hub for the Americas.

Mexico posted a trade surplus of US$9,857.3 million in the first six months of 2026. Total exports for the period reached US$389,723.3 million, a 24.6% increase compared to the first half of 2025.

What does the export record mean for foreign investors?

The data signals that Mexico is successfully capturing supply-chain relocation investment. The strong manufacturing performance and growing trade surplus suggest a stable foreign-exchange environment and expanding opportunities in industrial real estate, logistics, and supplier networks.

Drivers in Iraq's semiautonomous northern Kurdish region have been waiting for hours, and in some cases overnight, to buy petrol as a fuel crisis tightened its grip on Irbil. Most private petrol stations were shut on Tuesday, with only a few government-run outlets continuing to sell fuel.

The shortage has been linked by authorities to the ongoing conflict involving Iran. Kurdish regional government Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said on Monday that security threats, including drone attacks, had led Dana Gas, the biggest company in northern Iraq, to cut production at its Khor Mor gas field. He also urged the central government in Baghdad to raise the Kurdish region's allocation of crude oil for domestic use from 50,000 barrels a day to about 126,700 barrels to improve supplies and bring down prices.

Iran-backed Iraqi militia groups have carried out several drone strikes targeting American interests across Iraq, while the US has struck militia bases in response to defend its troops. Over the years, a number of Kurdish opposition groups have also taken up arms against the Iranian authorities, with some setting up bases in neighbouring Iraq. Those bases too have come under attack.

Mediators appear to be making progress in efforts to bring the US and Iran back to talks after both sides halted attacks following a period of sharply rising tensions. However, scattered attacks by armed groups have continued.

By 6 am on Tuesday, only a few stations were still dispensing fuel, and queues of cars had stretched so far that some drivers could no longer see the pumps they were waiting for. Many kept their windows slightly open to save every litre left in their tanks, choosing not to use air conditioning despite the intense summer heat. By mid-morning, temperatures had crossed 45 degrees Celsius, and men stood outside their vehicles with sweat-soaked shirts.

"We came at 11:30 p.m. last night," said Twana Mohammed, 43, a biology teacher, who left his car in the queue and returned before dawn. He said he had spent four days searching for fuel. "There's no fuel left in my car," he said. "It will be good if it makes it to the gas station."

At times, the frustration spilled into shouting matches as drivers abandoned single-file queues and formed two or even three lines. Abdullah Hamad, 50, a car dealer, said he had joined a queue at 5 am and was still waiting nearly three hours later. "Every five minutes we move forward a little bit, then turn the engine off, wait for five minutes, and move forward again," he said. He added that the shortage had cost people working hours.

At one of the few stations still operating, attendant Ameen Karwan, 25, said the station had received 36,000 litres of fuel that morning. By the time he spoke, workers had served about 300 vehicles and hoped the remaining supply would be enough for another 700 to 800. For now, he said, each family is limited to one fill-up of 40 litres twice a week.

Drivers said the shortage had worsened after regional authorities ordered lower pump prices, prompting many private stations to stop selling fuel rather than sell it at the mandated rate. Hamad pointed to the contradiction of long fuel queues in an oil-rich country. "Our country is full of oil. Our soil is full of oil," he said. Iraq depends on oil revenues for roughly 90 per cent of its budget.

Hamad said fuel had been expensive in Irbil even before the conflict between the US and Iran led to closures in the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway. But, he added, "We were even happy with the high price, as long as it's available." The crisis in Irbil has left residents spending long hours in queues as supply remains tight and only a small number of stations continue to operate.

  > Gold and silver prices faced selling pressure as investors awaited the US Federal Reserve's policy meeting. A stronger US dollar and rising interest rate expectations impacted precious metals, while geopolitical tensions eased, creating a complex market environment for investors.

Gold and silver prices came under renewed selling pressure on Tuesday, 28 July, as investors awaited the outcome of the US Federal Reserve's policy meeting, while a stronger US dollar weighed on precious metals by making them more expensive for holders of other currencies.

Comex gold futures fell $66 per troy ounce to an intraday low of $4,011, while silver futures also tumbled nearly $1.85 per troy ounce to $56.86.

The US Dollar Index traded around 101.5 against a basket of major currencies as markets priced in more than a one-third probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike later this year.

Since the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict in late February, expectations of higher interest rates have strengthened, keeping precious metals out of investors' favour as they do not offer any yield.

Interest-rate swaps currently imply about a one-in-three chance of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike, an unusually high degree of uncertainty this close to a Fed policy decision by the standards of recent years.

Those expectations have been shaped despite repeated calls from US President Donald Trump for lower interest rates. During June, US inflation came in lower than expected, aided by a decline in energy prices.

At its June policy meeting, the Federal Reserve kept the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.50%-3.75% for a fourth consecutive meeting. However, the central bank signalled that further policy tightening remains a possibility.

While precious metals are traditionally viewed as safe-haven assets during periods of geopolitical uncertainty, the sharp rise in crude oil prices has fuelled inflation concerns and increased the appeal of higher-yielding assets.

"Easing Middle East tensions after renewed US-Iran diplomatic engagement weighed on crude oil prices, tempering inflation concerns, although Trump warned military action could resume if talks fail," said domestic brokerage firm Kotak Securities.

Gold's near-term direction now hinges on the Fed's policy guidance and geopolitical developments, with a hawkish stance posing downside risks, while any renewed conflict could quickly revive safe-haven demand, the brokerage added.

The MCX silver futures contract dropped ₹6,324 per kg to an intraday low of ₹2,14,849. A break below the ₹2.10 lakh mark could push the white metal to its lowest level since late March.

- **2026-07-28** [Drones Repriced Global Energy And The Math Favors The Attacker](https://dronexl.co/2026/07/28/drones-repriced-global-energy-100-oil/) — DroneXL.co (relevance 0.25)
  > Brent crude settled above $100 a barrel on July 23, and the weapon most responsible for that number costs about $20,000 to build. Energy analysts are now saying out loud what DroneXL readers have watched unfold strike by strike since Operation Epic Fury opened on February 28: cheap, long-range drones have made it easier and dramatically cheaper to take refineries, tankers, and power grids offline, and the world's energy planners are being forced to redesign around that fact.

The wars in Ukraine and Iran are the proof of concept. Ukraine hits Russian refineries and export terminals almost daily. Iran used drones to choke shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and to damage Qatar's main LNG export hub. Gasoline averaged $4.09 a gallon in the U.S. last week, and analysts from Eurasia Group to Columbia now draw a straight line from those prices back to unmanned aircraft.

Anyone building energy infrastructure anywhere conflict is even remotely possible, Eurasia Group analyst Gregory Brew argues, now has to plan for drone defense. The rest of this story is about what that planning costs.

The Attacker's Math Beats The Defender's Budget

A Shahed-136 drone costs Russia roughly $20,000 per airframe, while the Patriot PAC-3 interceptor often used against incoming threats runs about $4 million per missile, a cost exchange so lopsided that defending every refinery, substation, and export terminal with missiles is an economic impossibility for any country. That figure comes from a Modern War Institute analysis published at West Point on July 8, which argues the economics of precision strikes have permanently tilted toward the attacker.

The production numbers make it worse. Russia can build 120 ballistic missiles a month. Current U.S. PAC-3 MSE output is about 600 a year, and even the Pentagon's push to more than triple that leaves little margin for missed intercepts. Saturation attacks will leak through. The MWI authors put it bluntly: "the grid is now effectively a frontline target."

The hardware on the receiving end compounds the problem. A single high-voltage autotransformer weighs over 200 tons, is built to order rather than stockpiled, and carries lead times exceeding 24 months. A drone that costs less than a used car can destroy equipment that takes two years to replace.

Ukraine Turned Russia's Refineries Into A Standing Target List

Ukrainian long-range strike drones now fly missions against Russian oil infrastructure on a near-daily basis, reaching targets from the Moscow region to the Baltic export terminals, and the campaign has grown from improvised harassment in 2024 into the systematic degradation of Russia's refining and export capacity. When Fire Point ran live footage of its Kapotnya refinery strike at its Eurosatory booth in June, the company's CEO said its FP-1 and FP-2 drones fly between 5 and 20 sorties into Russia every day.

The campaign's reach keeps growing. Ukraine's Liutyi drones hit the Ust-Luga terminal on the Gulf of Finland three times in a single week this spring, a stretch of the campaign that ended with a strike drone crashing in Finland with a live warhead. Russia felt those attacks in its own energy books, and the rest of the world felt them at the pump. Even Monday's price retreat came only after crude loadings resumed at a Black Sea terminal that Ukrainian drones had knocked offline.

Russia ran the same playbook in reverse against Ukraine's power grid, and the results were structural. A three-month wave of strikes in mid-2024 removed roughly nine gigawatts of generation, about half of Ukraine's winter peak demand, with direct damages now past $16 billion.

Iran Proved A Regional War Reprices Energy Worldwide

Iranian one-way attack drones turned the Strait of Hormuz, the 34-kilometer-wide (21-mile) chokepoint carrying about a fifth of the world's seaborne oil, into contested airspace for months, deterring tanker traffic despite overwhelming U.S. military superiority in the region. DroneXL documented that pattern in real time, including the day CENTCOM shot down four Iranian attack drones headed for the strait and answered with strikes on coastal radar sites.

Iranian drones also hit energy sites across the Gulf alongside missile salvos, including Qatar's main LNG export hub. Crude went from around $65 a barrel to above $100 during the spring closure of the strait, a spike DroneXL covered when Britain drew up plans to send minesweeping drones to reopen it. The strait reopened in June. The Houthis' Red Sea attacks last week sent Brent back over $100 anyway.

Energy Planners Now Design Grids Around The Drone Threat

Columbia energy scholar Tatiana Mitrova told Axios that infrastructure planning now requires completely different thinking, because a century of energy economics built around concentration and scale produced exactly the kind of massive, fixed, well-mapped targets that cheap drones are best at destroying. Her summary of the new logic: "the bigger the target, the bigger the damage."

The emerging playbook favors modular over monumental. Smaller distributed generation, microgrids that island themselves when the main grid takes a hit, blast walls and netting around transformers, buried control systems, and warm standby equipment. Ukraine is already living this doctrine, running mobile on-site power in response to Russian grid strikes. The MWI authors want the U.S. and its allies to adopt it before a war forces the issue, and they name Taiwan's centralized grid as the vulnerability a Chinese campaign would exploit first.

Washington Rewrote Counter-Drone Law And Skipped The Owners

A new federal framework took effect on July 1 that lets certified state and local law enforcement agencies track and in some cases disable threatening drones, yet the private companies that own America's refineries, pipelines, and substations still have no mitigation authority of their own. The SAFER SKIES Act, passed inside the FY 2026 defense bill in December, expanded DHS and DOJ counter-drone powers and ordered a certification framework for police and correctional agencies, which the two departments published as an interim final rule on July 6.

The rule does real things: two-tier certification separating detection from mitigation, an approved-technology list, spectrum coordination, air traffic notification. What it does not do is give a utility or refinery operator the right to act on its own. Jamming still violates FCC rules, and downing an aircraft, even a hostile quadcopter over your own transformer yard, remains a federal crime for a private operator.

The defense industry sees the market forming anyway. Lockheed Martin picked Fortem Technologies to field an autonomous counter-drone system for critical infrastructure protection in March. DroneShield and Terma partnered on layered counter-UAS for infrastructure customers in May. The demand signal is real. The legal authority for the customers who need it most is not.

DroneXL's Take

I've spent 2026 covering two wars that were fought and priced by drones, and the throughline is simpler than the think tanks make it: a $20,000 aircraft did what OPEC embargoes and sanctions regimes spent decades trying to do. It moved the global price of energy. Every gallon of $4 gas carries a drone premium, and that premium exists because attacking energy infrastructure got cheap while defending it stayed expensive.

Washington finally moved, and it moved in the wrong order. Three weeks ago the SAFER SKIES framework went live, giving police departments a path to counter-drone authority. Police departments don't own refineries. The West Point analysis names the actual target set, generation plants and export terminals, nearly all of it in private hands, and those owners got netting and blast walls. We've reported on surveillance drones methodically mapping German power plants and on unexplained incursions over U.S. installations. The threat model is documented. The people who own the targets still can't touch it.

The counter-drone industry isn't waiting. Lockheed, Fortem, DroneShield, Terma, and Honeywell have all announced infrastructure-protection systems in the past five months, and DroneXL has covered each one. The buyers with money and legal cover are militaries and Gulf states. The SAFER SKIES rule is interim, which means the framework is still being shaped, and how far the final version reaches beyond law enforcement decides whether American energy companies join that market or keep watching drones from behind a chain-link fence. The technology that repriced the world's energy is one the people who own the targets still aren't allowed to defend against. That should be a bigger story than the price of oil.

Source: Axios, Modern War Institute.

DroneXL uses automated tools to support research and source retrieval. All reporting and editorial perspectives are by Haye Kesteloo.
